{{Short description|American astronomer}}
'''John Craig Wheeler''' (born 1943)<ref>{{cite web |title=Wheeler, J. Craig |url=https://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n81126682.html |website=id.loc.gov |access-date=December 9, 2021}}</ref> is an American astronomer. He is the Samuel T. and Fern Yanagisawa Regents Professor of Astronomy Emeritus at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. He is known for his theoretical work on [[supernova]]e. He is a past president of the [[American Astronomical Society]], a Fellow of that society, and a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]].

==Early life and education==
Wheeler graduated from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1965 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in physics. He was awarded his PhD in physics in 1969 from the [[University of Colorado Boulder]].<ref name="Physics Today 2005">{{cite journal | title=Wheeler Elected President of AAS | journal=Physics Today | volume=58 | issue=7 | year=2005 | issn=0031-9228 | doi=10.1063/1.2012471 | pages=73}}</ref> He then held a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellowship]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] until 1971.<ref name="CV">{{citation |title=Curriculum Vitae - John Craig Wheeler |url=https://utdirect.utexas.edu/apps/student/coursedocs/nlogon/download/3442632 |publisher=University of Texas at Austin |accessdate=6 December 2021}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1971 Wheeler became an assistant professor in the Department of Astronomy at [[Harvard University]]. In 1974 he joined the Department of Astronomy at the University of Texas at Austin. He became the Samuel T. and Fern Yanagisawa Regents Professor of Astronomy in 1985.<ref name="CV" />

Wheeler served as the President of the American Astronomical Society (AAS) from 2006 to 2008. He was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 2007.<ref name="APS Fellow">{{cite web |title=APS Fellows Archive |url= https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=W |publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=7 December 2021}}</ref> In 2008, he became a Legacy Fellow of the AAS.<ref name="AAS Fellow">{{cite web |title=AAS Fellows |url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows |publisher=American Astronomical Society |access-date=7 December 2021}}</ref>

Based on the "Astronomy Bizarre" course he taught for non-majors, Wheeler published ''Cosmic Catastrophes: Supernovae, Gamma-ray Bursts, and Adventures in Hyperspace'' in 2000. The second edition,  ''Cosmic Catastrophes: Exploding Stars, Black Holes, and Mapping the Universe'', was published in 2007.<ref name="Physics Today 2005" /><ref>{{cite book | last=Wheeler | first=J.C. | title=Cosmic Catastrophes: Exploding Stars, Black Holes, and Mapping the Universe |edition=2nd | publisher=Cambridge University Press | year=2007 |orig-date=1st ed. 2000 |pages=xi–xiv| isbn=978-0-521-85714-7}}</ref> In 2019 he and David Branch received the Chambliss Astronomical Writing Award for their textbook ''Supernova Explosions''.<ref>{{cite web |title=AAS Names Recipients of 2019 Awards & Honors |url=https://aas.org/press/aas-names-recipients-2019-awards-honors |publisher=American Astronomical Society |date=2019 |access-date=9 December 2021}}</ref>
